newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end flat in thin, lethargic trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end flat in thin, lethargic trade.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed little changed in extremely weak, post-holiday trade as investors squared accounts and remained mostly sidelined ahead of the end of the year, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended flat at 98-28/32 to yield 6.59 percent. The two-year note was up 1/32 at 99-27/32, yielding 5.83 percent.
Volume was very light at $20.7 bilion by late trade as measured by GovPX. That is around 70 percent below average for a winter Thursday.
"There is nothing here. The market is dead, trading is dead, everything is dead," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "It's just post-Christmas hangover here."
GovPX said the little activity seen on Thursday was concentraded in the short-end of the yield curve, with bills accounting for 56 percent of the volume.
GovPX publishes real time Treasury prices and volume from five of the six intra-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the intra-dealer trades.
Analysts said some players were lured into Treasuries by an overall firm dollar tone against most major currencies.
Pundits said a rise in U.S. stocks kept the dollar well bid for most of the day, which in turn contributed to a somewhat bullish tone in the Treasury market.

Players were also encouraged by press reports saying the holiday shopping season might not be as strong as previously thought. The reports said post-holiday discounts were expected to help lift year-end profits.

"Based on my own personal observations going out to stores ... (holiday) traffic was heavy, but I didn't get the sense people were buying feverishly," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.

Possible weaker-than-expected Christmas sales are seen as a positive for bond traders. They said lower demand is likely to keep inflation in check by preventing retailers and manufacturers from sharply increasing prices.
Weaker oil prices on Thursday also bolstered Treasuries. The early drop in oil was tied to weak technicals and talk of low demand, traders said.
Analysts said money managers, hedge and pension funds were mostly out of the market. Retailers were seen sidelined. The little activity was seen focused on professional-led trades.
"There isn't really anything going on here. I wish I had something else to tell you, but it's very quiet," said another trader at a foreign investment bank here.

Analysts said Friday's session might bring some fresh news as the government releases jobless claims for the week ended December 21. In a Reuters survey, analysts expect the total to stand at 346,000 against 351,000 earlier.
The November durable goods report is also going to be released on Friday. The headline figure is expected to rise by 0.1 percent against a 0.3-percent jump in the previous month.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up three basis points at 4.98 percent. The six-month bill rate was unchanged at 5.06 percent. The year bill rate was flat at 5.20 percent.
The five-year note traded flat at 99-31/32 to yield 6.13 percent. The ten-year note closed unchanged at 101-4/32, yielding 6.34 percent.
